title: "Mrs" again
topic: Equality and fair treatment of patients
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in a gynaecology clinic. Mr Evans, 34, is a trans man attending about pelvic pain. His GP letter states his name and title clearly.

In the waiting room, a receptionist calls him "Mrs Evans", and a nurse uses the same title as she brings him into your room. He tells you quietly that this happens every time he comes, and that he nearly didn't come today.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Apologise to Mr Evans and use his correct name and title.
options.brief: Acknowledges what happened and shows respect.
options.detailed: A sincere apology recognises how distressing repeated misgendering can be, and using his correct name and title shows respect. It may help him feel able to keep attending.

options.text: Explain that the gynaecology system defaults to female titles.
options.brief: Explains the error, but treats it as acceptable.
options.detailed: Even if the system is a factor, the explanation sounds like an excuse and doesn't fix the problem.

options.text: Check his clinic record shows his correct name and title.
options.brief: An incorrect record may be causing the repeated errors.
options.detailed: Staff often read titles from the record. If it is wrong, correcting it, or asking the right team to, stops the problem at its source.

options.text: Tell him that the staff didn't mean to cause offence.
options.detailed: It may be true that no one intended offence, but saying so dismisses the impact, which is what matters to him.

options.text: Suggest he asks reception to update his details himself.
options.brief: Puts the burden on him after a distressing experience.
options.detailed: He has already been let down. It's the service's job to make sure records and practice are right.

options.text: Ask the clinic manager to make sure staff use his title.
options.brief: Prevents the same thing happening next time.
options.detailed: This has happened at every visit, so it needs addressing beyond today. Raising it constructively with the clinic manager helps make sure staff understand and change their practice.

options.text: Correct the nurse in front of Mr Evans as soon as she says it.
options.brief: Well meant, but may embarrass everyone, including him.
options.detailed: Public correction can draw more attention to him at a sensitive moment. A private word is usually more effective.

options.text: Refer him to a different clinic where staff may be more aware.
options.brief: Moves him away from the right clinic instead of fixing the problem.
options.detailed: He needs this clinic for his symptoms. Changing where he is seen avoids the problem rather than solving it.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you respond respectfully to a patient who has been repeatedly misgendered, and address the cause.
explanation.keyDetails: It happens every visit. His details are clear in the letter. He nearly didn't attend, which puts his care at risk.
explanation.reasoning: [A] apologises and shows respect, [C] fixes the record, and [F] addresses staff practice. The distractors excuse ([B], [D]), shift the burden ([E]), embarrass ([G]), or avoid the problem ([H]).
explanation.competing: [G] feels decisive, but correcting a colleague in front of the patient can make the moment harder for him. A private word with the clinic manager is more effective.

references.title: Equality Act 2010
references.note: Gender reassignment as a protected characteristic in the provision of services.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, treating patients with dignity and without discrimination.
